title: Non-smooth stochastic gradient descent using smoothing functions
contribution: Proposes smoothing stochastic gradient (SSG), plain SGD on a smoothing function f̃(·,µ_k) with µ_k driven to zero on a prescribed schedule, proves rates in convex (1/T^{1/4}), non-convex (close to T^{-1/2} for smoothing gradients, T^{-2/7+ε} for nearby subgradients) and strongly convex (close to 1/T^{1/2}) regimes, verifies the assumptions for two compositional problem classes, and reports preliminary tests on four UCI datasets (pp. 1, 5, 10, 13, 16, 33).
problem_entry: Stochastic compositional problems ϕ(E[ψ]) and E[ϕ(ψ)] with a non-smooth outer ϕ; SCGD targets inner non-smoothness, and no compositional method iteratively updates a smoothing parameter (pp. 1–4).
key_idea: SGD on f̃(·,µ_k) that only differs from SGD in the update µ_{k+1} ≤ µ_k; schedules µ_k = k^{-a}, α_k = k^{-b} fixed a priori by the rate analysis, (a,b) = (1/4,3/4) in the convex case, µ_k = α_k^{(2−d)/3} in the non-convex case (pp. 7, 10–11).
assumptions: Stated on f̃: unbiased gradients, second moment ≤ G²/µ², |f − f̃| ≤ Cµ; convex f̃ plus bounded iterates via projection; or ∇f̃ Lipschitz with C0/µ, Lipschitz in µ, Σα^d < ∞; a nearby-subgradient assumption for true subgradients. Verification for ϕ(E[ψ]) needs ϕ̃′ linear via restricted mean-preserving sampling and fails for the hinge case (pp. 7–8, 11, 14, 18–19).
proof_devices: projected-SGD distance recursion + convexity + telescoping with bounded iterates, then smoothing accuracy Cµ at x_k and x* (pp. 8–10)
LP maximizing min{a, 1−b, b−2a} over schedule exponents → (1/4, 3/4) (p. 10)
descent lemma with Lipschitz constant C0/µ_k plus µ-change term C1(µ_k − µ_{k+1}) (p. 12)
coupling µ_k = α_k^{(2−d)/3} so α_k²/µ_k³ = α_k^d is summable (pp. 11–13)
Lyapunov J_k = E‖x_k − x*‖² + Λ_k E‖y_k − ψ(x_{k−1})‖² with SCGD tracking lemma (pp. 35–37)
experiments: Finite-sum case only: hinge loss on QSAR and Breast Cancer Wisconsin, L1 loss on Automobile Price and Yacht Hydrodynamics, one 75/25 split, SSG vs non-smooth SGD and SCGD (run outside its assumptions) with the same α0 k^{-3/4} for all; test-loss curves, no repeated runs reported; SSG lowest final test loss and smoother curves (pp. 24–26).
positioning: Claims to match SCGD's rates for a 'complementary' problem (inner vs outer non-smoothness); dismisses a saddle-point O(T^{-1/2}) route as not convex–concave for nonlinear ψ; builds on own direct-search smoothing [18] (pp. 4, 10–11, 16).
writing: Assumptions introduced as 'mild' with forward promises of verification; strongly convex case relegated to an appendix as less applicable; each main result followed by an SCGD comparison; conclusion distils a design rule linking smoothing and step decay (pp. 7, 10, 16, 26–27).
limits_future: Stated: hinge case of (1.1) not covered, non-convex rates only for smoothing gradients/nearby subgradients, no double expectation; future: variance reduction (SVRG, SAGA), CVaR applications. Unstated: no code, convex proof does not use smoothness, O(1/√T) subgradient benchmark (p. 3) not addressed (pp. 16, 19, 27).

title: The limitation of neural nets for approximation and optimization
contribution: An empirical audit of neural networks as surrogates in optimization: SiLU is the best activation for approximating CUTEst objectives, NNs match interpolation/regression on values and gradients but not Hessians, an activation-augmented quadratic basis without cross terms is as accurate as the full basis, and NN or interpolation surrogate gradients do not improve the FLE derivative-free solver (pp. 1–3, 8, 15, 21).
problem_entry: NNs are popular engineering surrogates, but the authors know of no paper evaluating NN approximation accuracy or NN surrogates inside optimization algorithms (p. 2).
key_idea: Three-stage audit: activation choice via performance profiles of training, accuracy of value/gradient/Hessian against quadratic interpolation/regression and RBF on identical sample sets, then replace the forward-difference gradient in FLE's FD-BFGS step by a surrogate gradient (FLE-S) and profile against FLE (pp. 5–6, 11–12, 18–20).
assumptions: Smooth noiseless unconstrained f; samples uniform in B(x0;1), shifted and scaled; one NN architecture (2 hidden layers of 4n neurons, Adam, ReduceLROnPlateau monitoring the testing risk); no convergence theory (pp. 3, 6, 19).
proof_devices: none (no lemmas or theorems in the paper, checked pp. 1–31)
experiments: CUTEst sets of 38 problems (n = 20, 40, 60) and 53 negative-curvature problems (n = 2–50); performance profiles at τ = 10⁻², 10⁻⁵; relative-error box plots at x0; FLE vs FLE-S (natural basis, basis (3.5) with Sigmoid, RBF, NN-ReLU, NN-SiLU) in function evaluations; no FLE-S variant beats FLE; code on GitHub; no timings (pp. 3, 5–8, 12–17, 21).
positioning: Against engineering NN-surrogate practice and learning-to-optimize work; builds on DFO model literature and on evidence that FD-BFGS is strong for smooth noiseless DFO; baseline is the authors' own 'state-of-the-art' FLE (pp. 2–3, 8, 17).
writing: Verdict in the title and section headings; numbered contributions phrased as 'The evidence provided shows'; informal one-sentence summary of the negative result; positive by-product (cross terms dispensable) kept in the abstract; omitted failed variants disclosed in the conclusion (pp. 1–3, 15, 23).
limits_future: Stated: unit-ball sampling makes quadratic approximations inaccurate; a more complex NN argued (not tested) to remain uncompetitive. Unstated: single architecture, smooth noiseless problems only, n ≤ 60, no timing for the claimed training cost, no future work (pp. 6, 13, 15, 21–23).

title: Stochastic set-valued optimization and its application to robust learning
contribution: Introduces stochastic hyperbox-valued (interval- and rectangle-valued) optimization for robust learning, with sub- and superquantiles of the loss as lower and upper objectives of the equivalent multiobjective problem, proves a Rockafellar–Uryasev-type characterization for subquantiles, and solves the models with smoothed PF-SMG plus knee selection, reporting lower replication variance than ERM under class-proportion shift (pp. 1, 3–4, 11, 15–19, 23–24).
problem_entry: Robust ML reduces variability to a single empirical-risk measure, and set-valued optimization has no stochastic formulations (p. 3).
key_idea: Hyperbox SVO ≡ MOO with 2k objectives (Theorem 3.1); choose f_lb = subquantile and f_ub = superquantile of the loss, a family whose corners recover ERM and min–max; solve with PF-SMG with SSG smoothing and pick an angle-based knee (pp. 9, 11–12, 15).
assumptions: Hyperbox images (closed, convex S(x) ± K); ψ continuously differentiable; ξ independent of x; tail levels as hyperparameters; η replaced by the sorted empirical quantile; no convergence result for the pipeline (pp. 8, 11, 15, 19–20).
proof_devices: quantile reflection lemma Q_{−Z}(1−u) = −Q_Z(u) at continuity points (pp. 23–24)
S_p[Z] = −S̄_{1−p}[−Z] via change of variables, then Rockafellar–Uryasev applied to −Z (p. 24)
imported: Jahn's vectorization theorem and the hyperbox comparison of [21]/[11] (pp. 8–9)
experiments: Logistic regression on Adult (IVO, RVO) and German Credit (IVO); 1500 iterations, initial step 1.3, 30 class-rebalanced test replications from one test set; metrics: variance of test loss across replications and FRPA; baselines ERM, single SMG point, bi-objective knee; tail levels, smoothing and PF-SMG settings, accuracy values and code not reported in the text (pp. 15–18).
positioning: Careful SVO lineage (Kuroiwa, Khan–Tammer–Zălinescu, Hamel et al., Jahn, Eichfelder); criticizes robust ML approaches as a class; novelty claimed from the book and survey; reuses own SMG, PF-SMG, Pareto-sensitivity and SSG work; one citation slip ([26] for [25]) (pp. 2–3, 21).
writing: 'Our contributions' paragraph plus roadmap; first-person strong claim that any two-objective ML problem fits RVO; geometric intuition via Remark 5.1; hedging concentrated in the numerics; conclusion opens with a modelling lesson and ends with three concrete future directions (pp. 3–4, 13–14, 19–20).
limits_future: Stated future: more criteria (higher-dimensional hyperboxes), other knee rules targeting stability, data-driven tuning of tail levels. Unstated: no convergence theory, x_RVO is a weighted sum of two knees not shown Pareto optimal, one model class and two datasets, evaluation variance computed with model-specific losses (pp. 15–16, 19–20).
